strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important gap: evaluating multimodal reasoning over text-rich images rather than primarily measuring text extraction.
The benchmark covers 1,069 questions, six broad reasoning abilities, 18 task types, and several image sources, with both free-form and multiple-choice questions.
The empirical comparison is broad, covering proprietary and open-source MLLMs, OCR-plus-LLM pipelines, multiple model scales, and a chain-of-thought prompting ablation.
Annotating reasoning trajectories in addition to final answers could support useful process-level analysis if the annotations and evaluation protocol were validated more rigorously.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity is insufficiently established. The paper provides no inter-annotator agreement, category-agreement statistics, answer-audit results, rejection rates, or quantitative validation of annotation quality. Selecting between a human path and a Gemini-generated path conditioned on the answer can also produce post-hoc rationalizations rather than uniquely valid reasoning.

The manuscript itself exposes apparent annotation errors. In Figure 5, the reference solution enumerates 11 invertebrate groups but reports a final answer of 10. Figure 7's statistical-analysis example inconsistently states a subtotal of 787 and then computes using 789. Such errors materially undermine confidence in a benchmark of only 1,069 examples.

The reasoning metric is not reproducible or convincingly validated: the judge model, exact prompt, scoring scale and rubric, decoding settings, aggregation procedure, and agreement with human judgments are not reported. Comparing an output against one reference trajectory is especially questionable because many tasks admit multiple valid reasoning paths.

Final-answer evaluation is also underspecified. GPT-4o-based answer extraction and format-specific prompts may affect scores, but there is no extractor accuracy audit, sensitivity analysis, exact normalization specification, repeated-run variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

Construct validity and novelty are not fully convincing. Several categories mix OCR, ordinary visual counting, mathematical problem solving, and external knowledge; some handwritten examples are conventional problems merely photographed as images. The distinction from directly relevant benchmarks such as OCRBench v2 and Contextual is discussed only superficially, making the strong first/systematic-benchmark claim insufficiently supported.

The dataset contains 293 images from existing benchmarks and 476 Internet-sourced images, yet the paper does not adequately document deduplication, pretraining contamination, licenses, redistribution rights, provenance, privacy screening, or annotation compensation. These omissions also limit reproducibility and responsible release.

Several analyses overreach the evidence. For example, low OCR-plus-LLM performance does not isolate the importance of visual input because the compared language and multimodal models are not controlled counterparts. Likewise, conclusions about reinforcement learning are confounded by different base models, data, architectures, and parameter counts.

Presentation and reproducibility need substantial improvement: the abstract ends with an incomplete release statement, model/API versions and decoding parameters are missing, the judge prompt and evaluation scripts are not included in the manuscript, and some qualitative discussion contradicts the displayed outputs. Overall, the promising benchmark idea is not yet supported by the quality control and evaluation rigor expected at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The benchmark targets an important and timely gap: reasoning over text-rich images is not adequately characterized by conventional OCR/VQA accuracy alone.
The taxonomy covers six abilities and 18 practical task types. The dataset contains 1,069 mostly newly collected questions, including both free-form and multiple-choice formats.
The evaluation includes a reasonably broad set of proprietary, open-source, and OCR-plus-LLM systems, with category-level results and a chain-of-thought comparison.
The qualitative examples are useful for illustrating possible perception and reasoning failures.
weaknesses: Inspection of the complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/b534cac515cc4017995fbdf79a45d9ef/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} reveals major benchmark-validity issues. The annotation process selects between only two rationales—one human-written and one Gemini-generated—using subjective scores, but reports no rubric, agreement statistics, adjudication results, human-performance estimate, or systematic correctness audit.

The paper itself exposes questionable ground truth. In Figure 5, the reference answer counts 11 invertebrate groups while mixing the parent category “Arthropods” with four child categories. The question is also ambiguous about whether groups or depicted animals should be counted. Such examples directly weaken confidence in the labels.

Table 1 states that all 1,069 answers are unique, which is implausible given the 250 multiple-choice questions. This suggests that the statistic may conflate final answers with full reasoning trajectories or otherwise be incorrectly defined.

Reasoning-path evaluation is neither reproducible nor validated. The judge model, prompt, scoring scale, decoding settings, aggregation method, and treatment of alternative valid reasoning paths are unspecified. No agreement with human judgments is measured.

The central modality claim is based on a confounded comparison: PP-OCRv3 plus separate language models is compared with end-to-end MLLMs. OCR quality, layout preservation, language-model capability, and modality all change simultaneously. Perfect-OCR and same-backbone image-versus-text controls are missing.

Accuracy below 50% does not by itself demonstrate difficult reasoning. Errors could arise from OCR failures, ambiguous questions, incorrect annotations, or specialized knowledge. The study provides no human ceiling, difficulty calibration, perception-versus-reasoning decomposition, or representative label-quality audit.

The novelty claims are overstated. Closely related cited benchmarks—including Contextual, OCRBench v2, ChartQA, and MME-Finance—are not differentiated through a precise comparison of tasks, annotations, evaluation protocols, and coverage.

Reproducibility is weak: exact prompts are not fully provided; model/API versions and evaluation dates are absent; decoding and image-processing settings are missing; answer-extraction details are vague; and the promised benchmark/code URL is blank.

The evaluation reports only point estimates, without confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated runs, or per-task sample counts. Conclusions about reinforcement-learning methods are especially speculative because controlled paired baselines are not provided.

There are concrete inconsistencies in the analysis. The CoT discussion repeats GPT-4o where MM-Eureka appears intended. More seriously, the Figure 6 discussion claims Qwen and DouBao interpreted “6 jumbo shrimp” as six separate items, although their displayed calculations use the price of one listed dish; their evident error is including the already purchased salad.

The dataset is imbalanced, with 37% of examples assigned to numerical analysis. Its use of unspecified internet repositories and prior benchmarks also raises unresolved contamination, licensing, privacy, and redistribution concerns. The paper contains no meaningful ethics or data-governance discussion.

Overall, the topic and experimental breadth are promising, but the label ambiguity, unvalidated reasoning metric, confounded baselines, reproducibility gaps, and unsupported claims are substantive. A major benchmark audit and evaluation redesign would be required for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important gap: reasoning over text-rich images is less systematically evaluated than OCR extraction or visual mathematics.

Introduces 1,069 human-curated examples spanning six reasoning abilities and 18 task types, with broad coverage of documents, charts, photographs, handwritten problems, and everyday decision scenarios.
Evaluates a wide range of closed- and open-source models, includes OCR-plus-LLM comparisons, and studies chain-of-thought prompting and model scaling.
The main empirical finding—that current MLLMs remain weak on these tasks—is clearly presented and supported by informative category-level results and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: Benchmark quality is not validated rigorously enough. The paper omits annotator counts, annotation and adjudication rubrics, inter-annotator agreement, human performance, difficulty calibration, and systematic error auditing. Some displayed examples are themselves ambiguous or questionable, such as the animal-classification reference that appears to count both a parent class and its subclasses.

The reasoning-path evaluation is substantially underspecified: the judge model, exact prompt, score definition, sampling settings, and aggregation procedure are not reported. There is also no human agreement study or robustness analysis for the judge, despite reasoning-path assessment being a central claimed contribution.

Final-answer evaluation relies on an LLM extractor followed by incompletely described normalization. Extractor accuracy is not validated, and the claim of deterministic evaluation is therefore insufficiently supported. Format-specific prompts additionally reveal answer structure and may affect models unevenly.

Several conclusions are stronger than the experimental evidence. The OCR-plus-LLM comparison confounds modality with OCR quality and model choice, so it does not isolate the value of visual input. Claims about reinforcement learning are based on a small, heterogeneous collection of methods without controlled base-model comparisons.

The benchmark is modest in size and partly derived from existing datasets and public internet images, but the paper provides no contamination analysis, licensing discussion, source-level performance breakdown, or safeguards against near-duplicate content. Ethical and privacy considerations are also absent.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate for a benchmark paper: important model versions, inference parameters, image preprocessing details, prompts, judge configuration, and evaluation scripts are not documented in the manuscript. No confidence intervals or significance testing are reported.

Presentation contains factual and editorial inconsistencies, including contradictory qualitative discussion of the “6 jumbo shrimp” example, an erroneous CoT-improvement sentence, unclear dataset statistics such as 1,069 unique answers, and an incomplete resource-availability statement. Overall, the idea and experimental breadth are promising, but unresolved validity and reproducibility issues prevent acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap: evaluating reasoning over text-rich images rather than only OCR or direct answer extraction.
The benchmark covers 1,069 examples, six broad reasoning categories, 18 practical task types, and several image sources, including real-world photographs and handwritten material.
Providing both final-answer and step-by-step reasoning annotations is potentially valuable for diagnosing model failures beyond exact-answer accuracy.
The empirical study is broad, covering many closed-source, open-source, reasoning-oriented, and document-oriented models, with category-level results and some prompting ablations.
The paper includes useful initial analyses of OCR-only input, chain-of-thought prompting, few-shot prompting, model scaling, and error types.
weaknesses: Dataset reliability is insufficiently established. Annotation rubrics, annotator agreement, adjudication criteria, audit sample sizes, and quality-control outcomes are not reported quantitatively. Visible examples contain inconsistencies: Figure 8's reference explanation says there are 11 groups but gives a final answer of 10, and several questions or category assignments appear ambiguous.

The reasoning-process metric is under-specified. The judge model, prompt, scoring rubric, and score scale are not clearly documented. Validation reports only aggregate scores for four systems, without sample size, correlations, inter-rater agreement, or per-example analysis; model-generated reference paths may also introduce circularity when related models serve as judges.

Central causal claims are not supported by controlled comparisons. The conclusion that image input is crucial compares OCR-plus-LLM systems against different multimodal architectures, confounding visual access with backbone, training, and OCR quality. A same-model image-versus-OCR ablation or oracle-transcription condition is needed.

Reproducibility is weak: the abstract's resource URL is empty, and the appendix states that the benchmark and code will be released in the future. Important inference settings, image resolution, decoding parameters, API/model versions, judge prompts, extraction prompts, and normalization rules are missing.

The evaluation may leak answer structure through per-instance format prompts such as '$ + Integer'. The effect of this assistance is not ablated, and normalization for free-form strings is not specified sufficiently for a deterministic benchmark.

The novelty and positioning are overstated. Related benchmarks that already include text-rich visual reasoning, including OCRBench v2, MME-Finance, CharXiv, and VisuLogic, are cited but not compared carefully in terms of task composition, required reasoning, annotation quality, or metric design.

Source-image contamination is not analyzed despite reusing 293 images from established benchmarks and retaining some non-new questions. There is no deduplication, memorization audit, or discussion of whether evaluated models encountered these images during training.

The six-category taxonomy is heterogeneous and does not cleanly isolate abilities: perception, OCR, arithmetic, domain knowledge, commonsense, and reasoning remain entangled. Some examples, such as genealogy under spatial reasoning, expose questionable construct validity.

Statistical rigor is limited: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run variability are reported. The error analysis omits its sample size and annotation protocol, and its displayed category percentages sum to 101%.

The synthetic-data experiment provides only a small 1.3-point overall gain while substantially degrading some categories, yet the paper draws a broad conclusion about the curation framework's utility without controls, variance estimates, or training details.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating reasoning over text-rich images rather than only OCR or answer retrieval.
OCR-Reasoning has useful breadth, with 1,069 examples over 1,022 images, six reasoning categories, 18 practical tasks, multiple image sources, and both free-form and multiple-choice questions.
Providing reference reasoning paths in addition to final answers could support process-level analysis and future reward-model research.

The empirical survey covers a broad collection of closed-source, open-source, reasoning-oriented, and document-oriented models, with additional CoT, few-shot, error-analysis, and synthetic-fine-tuning experiments.

The manuscript is generally readable, and its main tables and taxonomy figures communicate the intended benchmark structure clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3c79a02e4ff9431aad14143e6bcc1b4a/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The benchmark's annotation reliability is not convincing. Concrete apparent errors survive the claimed manual review: the family-tree example answers “great-grandson” when the question asks for the ancestor's relation to the descendant, which should be “great-grandfather”; the statistical-analysis example inconsistently switches from 787 to 789; and the error-analysis percentages sum to 101.0%. Table 1's claim of 1,069 unique answers is also implausible as stated given 250 multiple-choice questions.

Dataset construction lacks essential documentation: there is no annotation rubric, annotator count beyond per-example voting, inter-annotator agreement, qualification study, compensation information, rejection rate, audit sample, or systematic estimate of residual answer/reasoning errors. Selecting the “highest-quality” question from proposals may also introduce uncontrolled difficulty and selection bias.

The novelty and positioning are overstated. Closely related benchmarks such as OCRBench v2, Contextual, ChartQA, MME-Finance, and other document/chart reasoning datasets already study substantial parts of text-rich visual reasoning. The six-way taxonomy is generic, overlapping, and unsupported by agreement statistics, while the paper sometimes inaccurately characterizes prior datasets—especially ChartQA—as mere extraction benchmarks.

The central OCR-versus-image conclusion is not established by a controlled experiment. The paper compares PP-OCRv3 plus one language model against differently trained multimodal models and even calls DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B and Qwen2.5-VL-32B the “same LLM.” Differences can arise from model training, architecture, or the chosen OCR system. A paired ablation using the same model with image, OCR, and oracle transcription inputs is needed.

Reasoning-process evaluation is under-specified and potentially biased. The judge model, prompt, scoring scale, and aggregation procedure are not reported; a single reference trajectory may penalize valid alternative reasoning; and some references are model-generated. The human validation gives only four aggregate scores, without sample size, correlations, confidence intervals, agreement measures, or blinded evaluation.

Experimental reproducibility is poor. The abstract's repository link is blank, while the appendix says the benchmark and code will be released in the future. Model versions, access dates, decoding settings, image preprocessing/resolution, answer-normalization rules, numerical tolerances, prompts, and inference details are incomplete or absent.

Several analyses do not adequately support their claims. Table 6 places incompatible metrics on one scale (e.g., OCRBench scores around 860 versus percentages elsewhere); no uncertainty or significance estimates are given; few-shot gains of only 0.4–0.7 points may correspond to a handful of examples; and the synthetic fine-tuning experiment omits training details and shows regressions in major categories despite the positive conclusion.

Contamination and provenance are insufficiently addressed. The benchmark reuses 293 images from established datasets, includes 82 questions that are not newly collected, and draws 476 images from unspecified internet sources, but provides no split provenance, deduplication or contamination analysis, licenses, permissions, privacy review, or handling policy for potentially sensitive real-world photographs.

Overall, the task and breadth are promising, but the demonstrated label inconsistencies, weak validation, confounded central comparisons, incomplete release, and overstated positioning prevent this version from being a trustworthy top-tier benchmark contribution. These are substantial issues rather than presentation-only defects.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: evaluating reasoning, rather than only text recognition, in text-rich images. The taxonomy spanning six abilities and 18 practical tasks is useful and reasonably broad.

The benchmark includes 1,069 examples with both final-answer and reasoning-path annotations, mostly based on newly written questions, and covers documents, charts, photographs, handwriting, and real-world decision tasks.

The empirical study is extensive, covering closed-source, open-source, reasoning-oriented, and document-specialized models. Per-category results, chain-of-thought and few-shot studies, reasoning scores, and an error analysis provide several informative views of current limitations.

The finding that strong OCR/document models remain weak on these tasks is potentially valuable, and the comparison of OCR-plus-LLM and multimodal inputs helps motivate preserving visual layout and structure.
The paper is generally well organized, and the benchmark construction pipeline and high-level evaluation protocol are understandable.
weaknesses: Benchmark quality is not validated rigorously enough for a dataset paper. There is no reported human ceiling, independent audit error rate, inter-annotator agreement, ambiguity rate, or category-wise quality analysis. Several displayed examples themselves appear problematic: the genealogy example reverses the requested relationship in its final answer, the mathematical odd-function derivation contains sign inconsistencies, and a statistical example alternates between totals of 787 and 789. These visible errors weaken confidence in the full benchmark.

The reasoning-path evaluation, a central claimed contribution, relies on an underspecified LLM judge and comparison against a single reference trajectory. The judge model, complete rubric and prompt, decoding configuration, and robustness to alternative valid reasoning paths are not provided. Human validation reports only four aggregate scores, without sample size, annotator agreement, correlations, or uncertainty estimates.

Reproducibility is currently limited. The manuscript says the benchmark and scripts are available, but no usable anonymized link is shown, while the appendix describes release as future work. Important details such as model/API versions, decoding settings, image preprocessing, complete prompts, per-example predictions, and confidence intervals are also absent.

The comparison with OCR-plus-LLM does not cleanly establish that image input itself is essential: it combines modality changes with PP-OCRv3 recognition errors and loss of layout, and compares models with different capabilities. Oracle transcription and structured OCR/layout baselines would better isolate perception, layout understanding, and reasoning.

Novelty relative to OCRBenchV2, Contextual, Seed-Bench-2-Plus, and other text-rich visual-reasoning benchmarks is asserted more strongly than demonstrated. A systematic task-overlap comparison and evaluation on the closest competing reasoning benchmarks are needed.

The dataset mixes Internet images, newly photographed material, and images reused from existing benchmarks, but image licenses, redistribution permissions, privacy screening, source-level composition, duplication checks, and contamination risks are not adequately documented.

The annotation description is incomplete: the number and qualifications of annotators, compensation, scoring rubric, acceptance thresholds, disagreement resolution, and proportion of selected human versus model-generated reasoning paths are missing. Calling every example human-annotated is potentially misleading when model-generated paths may be selected after human review.

Several conclusions overreach the evidence. Low accuracy alone does not establish that failures arise from reasoning rather than ambiguous questions, annotation errors, perception failures, or formatting sensitivity; the error taxonomy is reported for only one model and lacks annotation methodology or agreement statistics.
